analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of Northern Rockies national forests from roadbuilding, logging, mining, and drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill died without any vote: introduced with four cosponsors in the final weeks of the 102nd Congress, it sat in three House committees and three subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act would have designated roughly 14 million acres of national forest land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness and biological connecting corridors, added dozens of rivers to the Wild and Scenic Rivers system, and barred new roads, logging, mining, and oil and gas development in the protected areas. It also would have created a Forest Service 'Wildlands Recovery Corps' to restore damaged forest land, and directed studies of new national parks at Hells Canyon and the Flathead country. All of this land is already federal public land; the bill changed what it could be used for.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or values federal public lands in the Northern Rockies: hikers, anglers, hunters, and local tourism economies would keep large roadless wild areas intact. Downstream communities benefit from watershed protection, since the bill's findings note these forests supply clean water to much of the continent. The bill also created restoration jobs through a new Wildlands Recovery Corps.

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness across seven named ecosystems — including Greater Yellowstone, Greater Glacier/Continental Divide, and the Greater Salmon country — protecting habitat for grizzly bears, wolves, caribou, and salmon and trout runs, which the bill text notes exist intact nowhere else south of Canada [S3].

Prohibits new road construction, even-aged timber harvesting, mining, and oil and gas development in biological connecting corridors, with road density capped near zero miles per square mile, while expressly exempting dozens of named federal, state, and county highways so existing access stays open [S3].

Creates a Wildlands Recovery Corps within the Forest Service to restore damaged forest land to native cover, stabilize eroding slopes, and reopen fish spawning runs — a jobs program funded by appropriations [S2].
Protects rivers by designating dozens of segments as wild and scenic rivers and freezing new roads, dams, logging, mining, and drilling along studied streams until Congress decides their status [S2].

Directs Interior to study new national parks at Hells Canyon/Chief Joseph and the Flathead, and withdraws the Badger-Two Medicine area from mining while affirming Blackfeet Nation treaty rights and guaranteeing Native American access for cultural and religious uses [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies lose access to roadless areas they currently log (often at a loss to the Treasury, per the bill's own findings); mining and oil and gas companies lose acreage open to entry and leasing; some motorized recreation would be restricted in corridors. Taxpayers would fund the land purchases and restoration program the bill authorizes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas industries

drawbacks.text: Restricting roadless-area logging would reduce timber supply and cost jobs in rural logging communities in Idaho, Montana, and surrounding states — the bill's own findings concede that development of roadless areas continues under current management, meaning this bill would have ended that activity in these specific areas [S3].

Mining and oil and gas interests lose access to lands currently open under the mining and mineral leasing laws, including a full withdrawal of the Badger-Two Medicine area from all mineral entry and geothermal leasing [S2].

Some users would lose access: motorized recreation is curtailed in corridor lands and the bill authorizes federal purchase of private inholdings, requiring sellers to relinquish mineral and water rights [S2].

The bill was enormous and administratively heavy — millions of acres across five states with detailed management mandates — and opponents could fairly argue that local and state voices, and industries dependent on multiple use, had little role in its acre-by-acre design [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — keeping the last large intact ecosystem south of Canada whole, protecting headwaters, and restoring damaged forests — was large and permanent, while the costs fell on a concentrated set of extractive industries and some rural timber jobs. The tradeoff was real for timber-dependent towns, but the bill itself argued that roadless logging in these areas returned less to the Treasury than it cost taxpayers. The bigger question was scale and process: this was a region-wide decision made in Washington rather than through the forest-by-forest planning process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 1992, three months before Congress adjourned, referred to three committees and then three subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it — so it never reached a House vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Peter Kostmayer of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on September 15, 1992, joined by two Democrats and two Republicans as original cosponsors [S1].

The same day, it was referred to three House committees — Agriculture, Interior and Insular Affairs, and Merchant Marine and Fisheries — the standard route for a bill touching Forest Service, wildlife, and public-lands jurisdiction [S5].
In October 1992 it went to three subcommittees (Forests, Fisheries and Wildlife, and National Parks and Public Lands), and no committee ever held a markup or sent it to the floor [S5].
The bill attracted only four cosponsors total — two Democrats and two Republicans — and never received a vote in either chamber before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests were better off because the bill died: roadless national forest acreage in five states stayed open to roadbuilding, logging, and mineral entry, and no hearing or vote was ever held on the protections.

for.name: Rep. Peter H. Kostmayer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original bipartisan cosponsor group.

for.name: Reps. Sherwood Boehlert and James Walsh (R) and Gerry Sikorski and Jim Jontz (D)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its original bipartisan supporters; no further recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — two Democrats and two Republicans joined the Democratic sponsor — but with only four cosponsors and no votes ever taken, no partisan pattern of support or opposition appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill bars logging and even-aged harvest in newly designated wilderness and corridors across five states, removing roadless acreage from the timber supply. The bill's findings argue that roadless logging in these forests frequently cost taxpayers more than it returned, so the industry's loss was partly a public gain [S3].
Mining is prohibited in corridors and park study areas, and the Badger-Two Medicine area is withdrawn from all mining entry and geothermal leasing [S2].
The bill bars oil and gas leasing in corridors and study areas, and requires buyers of purchased inholdings to relinquish federal oil and gas leases [S2].
A new Wildlands Recovery Corps in the Forest Service would be hired and equipped to restore damaged lands — jobs funded by public appropriations [S2].
Protected wild land, rivers, and potential new national parks would support recreation economies in the region; hunting and fishing are preserved in proposed preserve classifications [S2].
